--- ARRAYS: TWO POINTERS & SLIDING WINDOW ---


Arrays are the most fundamental data structure. Two Pointers is an algorithmic technique that uses two indices to iterate through a sequence. It is often used to search for pairs in a sorted array or to reverse elements. Sliding Window is a sub-technique of two pointers used to track a subset of data (a window) that moves through the array to find subarrays that meet specific criteria (like maximum sum or smallest length).

--- LINKED LISTS ---


A Linked List consists of nodes where each node contains data and a reference to the next node. Common operations include insertion, deletion, and traversal. Techniques like the 'Fast and Slow' pointer (Hare and Tortoise) are crucial for detecting cycles or finding the middle element.

--- STACKS AND QUEUES ---


Stacks follow LIFO (Last-In-First-Out) logic, essential for expression evaluation and backtracking. Queues follow FIFO (First-In-First-Out) logic, used in breadth-first search and task scheduling. Monotonic stacks are a specialized use-case to find the next greater or smaller element.

--- GREEDY ALGORITHMS ---


Greedy algorithms build up a solution piece by piece, always choosing the next piece that offers the most obvious and immediate benefit. While they don't always produce the globally optimal solution, they are efficient for problems like Huffman Coding or Fractional Knapsack.

--- RECURSION AND BACKTRACKING ---


Recursion is a method where the solution to a problem depends on solutions to smaller instances of the same problem. Backtracking is a refinement of recursion used for searching all possible solutions (like N-Queens or Sudoku) by abandoning paths that fail to satisfy constraints.

--- DYNAMIC PROGRAMMING ---


Dynamic Programming (DP) optimizes recursive solutions by storing the results of subproblems (memoization or tabulation). It is applied to problems with overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure, such as the Longest Common Subsequence or Edit Distance.
